title: Why did Nepal’s mountain agenda stall at COP31? A delegation insider explains - The Kathmandu Post
description: Why did Nepal’s mountain agenda stall at COP31? A delegation insider explains  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal went to COP31 with the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli floods behind it and a plain ask: give mountains a permanent place in the UN climate talks. On October 29, Nepal and Bhutan jointly proposed a COP31 agenda item on “1.5°C warming in mountains”. It did not make the formal agenda.

With negotiators now bargaining over the wording of the conference’s cover decision, Nepal is pressing for a dedicated mountain work programme with a defined scope, an annual high-level dialogue, and finance that arrives on time.

Avishek Shrestha, adviser to Minister for Agriculture, Forests and Environment Gita Chaudhary, is inside that process. Chaudhary now leads the delegation. Shrestha spoke to The Post ’s Biken K Dawadi from the negotiations, to explain why the proposal stalled, why consensus politics cuts against small mountain countries, what $20 million from the Loss and Damage Fund can and cannot do, and what Nepal would count as a win.

Reports say the mountain proposal was dropped from the official negotiating papers. What happened?

It was not dropped. Let me start from the beginning. On October 29, Nepal and Bhutan jointly submitted a mountain agenda item titled “1.5°C warming in mountains.” Countries usually submit agenda items so that a subject can be discussed in depth at the COP. This year Nepal and Bhutan did, as did other countries. In the last five or six years, no such specific agenda item has been approved.

What did the submission ask for?

Four things. First, a work programme on mountains. Second, an annual high-level dialogue on mountains and climate change. Third, scientific understanding and research on 1.5°C warming in mountains. Fourth, mountain-specific priorities: an adaptation framework, climate finance under the New Collective Quantified Goal, and loss and damage.

What happened after the submission?

The submissions came together as a provisional agenda. On November 8, the day before the plenary, the presidency called all the parties in. Kyrgyzstan had made its own submission on a mountain-related dialogue, and it was almost the same as ours. Kyrgyzstan also leads the Mountain Group, about sixteen countries, which Nepal has joined. So we merged. Kyrgyzstan added its submission to ours, and we pushed together.

How hard did Nepal push?

Our political leadership told us to fight for this agenda, and Minister Chaudhary led that fight. There are two presidencies this time, for the first time. Australia leads the negotiations, and Türkiye handles the logistics and engagement with participants. We told them plainly that if the agenda was not endorsed, we would raise a point of order.

Why does a point of order matter?

Under the UNFCCC, decisions are consensus-based, unlike the UN General Assembly, where voting is the norm. Any single country that objects can stop a session. A point of order from us would have halted the plenary on the ninth. The message was that this issue matters to us. After the Bhotekoshi flood, the world saw what climate change can do, including the loss of lives, among them people from countries other than Nepal. That event drew global attention, and it is why a formal mountain agenda should exist.

Whom did you have to convince?

Everyone. Negotiations here happen through blocs, and there are around sixteen. We negotiate mainly through the Least Developed Countries and the G77 and China, and we spoke to the Arab Group, the African Group and the Latin American bloc, AILAC. The European Union and other developed-country groups, including the Environmental Integrity Group with Switzerland, are also in the room. Then there is the LMDC, the Like-Minded Developing Countries, where India and China sit together.

So where did it land?

It did not become a formal agenda item, but we did not walk away empty. The title was a sticking point. “1.5°C warming in mountains” made some countries uncomfortable, because they read it as heavier obligations for themselves. Nepal, Bhutan and Kyrgyzstan agreed to revise it to “matters relating to mountains and climate change.” It is broader, and it is easier for other groups to join.

An agenda item cannot happen now, but we agreed on how to bring it to the next COP. It will be discussed in the COP presidency’s consultations, which took place in the first week and continue next week.

And the annual dialogue?

We were told it would be taken up at the subsidiary bodies, SB66 and SB68, which meet in Bonn, where the UNFCCC secretariat is headquartered, every June. That means June 2027 and June 2028. That is what was offered to us.

Bonn in 2028 sounds like a long wait. Is this a defeat dressed up as continuity?

I would not call it that. The process runs in parallel, and we are still fighting for the agenda. Remember, we asked for more than consultations. A presidency consultation alone is not enough, because the real weight lies in the cover decision. That is the high-level political decision the COP endorses. We have repeatedly asked that our asks appear there as outcome text, and not only in the presidency’s consultations.

What does the draft cover decision say?

A draft came out yesterday. It acknowledges the impacts on mountains. It also calls for a dedicated mountain work programme on finance and capacity-building gaps. But that falls short of what we asked for.

So Nepal, Bhutan and Kyrgyzstan made another submission. We want the text to say explicitly what the scope and modalities of the mountain work programme are. We want the annual mountain dialogue linked to that programme and guided by its framework. Nepal made a separate submission calling for a high-level political dialogue on mountains and climate change every year.

Did the presidencies hear you?

Minister Chaudhary met Chris Bowen, Australia’s lead negotiator, and Murat Kurum, a minister from Türkiye, who is both head of delegation and chief negotiator. The first meeting was at 9:30 pm, and we sat with the Turkish side from about 10:30 until nearly midnight. We told them this is an event the world has not seen before, that there is global sympathy, that our people expect results, and that the Prime Minister raised it at the UN General Assembly. We also said the mountain agenda is not confined to mountains. It connects to coastal regions and the seas.

Both gave us assurances of support. They said they would consider how to reflect our concerns. Next week the minister meets ministers from the EU, the big developing countries, the developed countries and the small island states. The process runs through next week.

Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal has returned home, and Minister Chaudhary now leads the delegation. Does that change anything?

Technically, a country can have two heads of delegation. Minister Khanal led the whole team until the 13th, and the handover has been made. Minister Chaudhary now leads the delegation through the end of the first week and the second. It changes nothing in the leadership.

Nepal’s climate diplomats have been busy with side events, including the cryosphere event with Bhutan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Pakistan. Yet the negotiating room does not seem to convert that into support. Why?

Because voting is not the practice. Article 18 of the Convention gives each party one vote, but in practice decisions have always been made by consensus. If any country is unhappy, it can object, so everything goes through consensus.

Developed countries have their own interests. We have not yet found the support and solidarity we wanted. But a dedicated mountain work programme has come, and the agenda will still be discussed in the presidency’s consultations.

Minister Khanal said in an interview that big negotiators and blocs blocked it. Are they the same people you meet on the sidelines?

The discomfort I described over the 1.5°C title is part of it. We have been meeting ministers one-on-one, including from developed countries. They know the gravity of the issue, and many have diplomatic offices in our countries. That has to be reflected in actual climate diplomacy. Next week we have more homework. The meetings so far have been positive, but in the end we have to go home with something substantial. The damage is irreversible, and the cost of rebuilding is enormous.

The Loss and Damage Fund has allocated $20 million for Nepal, yet nothing has been disbursed, and Kathmandu has not sent a formal proposal. Why is Nepal struggling on this front?

It is $21.6 million: $20 million for the work and $1.6 million for operational costs. It came from the first-ever extraordinary meeting of the fund. The government has started a process, and we are discussing it. In a day or two, the proposal work will begin in earnest.

The question is how to use the money most effectively. $20 million is not a lot, but I think it can become a global case study. If we use it well, other countries can receive money this way too, and we could draw in more resources.

The board meets in the Philippines around December 10 to 12, and we want clarity before then. In the coming days, we will consult ministries and other stakeholders on the financing mechanism and the kinds of projects. By the end of the week, we should have something we can share with the media.

As you said, $20 million is meagre against the cost of reconstruction. I understand about 119 countries have applied to the fund, and the applications total many times its money.

The need is far greater than the money. The fund pledged about $800 million, and barely $400 million has come in. Minister Chaudhary raised this at the fund’s high-level event, and we sit with its board again next week.

For a country like Nepal, the rebuilding bill runs to around 20 percent of GDP. The figure so far is about $4.7 billion. That is why the fund must grow substantially. We are pressing, politically and diplomatically, for money that is accessible, timely and affordable. If the $20 million had come a little earlier, or later, the question of how to use it would have been different. We told Türkiye and Australia that it is not only about the mountain agenda. It is also about resources.

The United States is absent from COP31, and Australia has not put forward new multi-year climate finance. Traditional donors are stepping back. How is Nepal adjusting its finance diplomacy?

On finance, honestly, there is very little. Even the money that was pledged has not arrived, and the fund’s shortfall shows it. Countries have also backed out of decisions they already agreed to. The Baku goal calls for $300 billion a year by 2035, and tripling adaptation finance was also agreed. Neither is being delivered.

Meanwhile, huge sums go into fossil fuel subsidies and into war. Taken together, it is something like three to four trillion dollars globally. Climate change has become tied to geopolitics. Countries are fuelling the crisis, which began mainly with historical emitters, and people are dying.

Our position is clear. The government’s priority is grant-based finance, and in every country statement and intervention we say “grant-based.” We work through the G77 and China to strengthen the finance negotiation, and the minister is holding bilateral meetings with other developing countries on how to hold this ground. Money for fossil fuel subsidies and military wars has to come to save humanity, and the people who have done nothing to cause this crisis.

The delegation also met UN Secretary-General António Guterres on the sidelines. What can Nepal expect from him?

He has been a big ambassador for the mountains. When he came to Nepal a few years ago, what he said about the Himalaya sensitised people globally. He is a true advocate.

In our meeting, we spoke with respect for what he has already said. After this disaster, he spoke at an overarching level. A person of his stature who has seen the gravity and the first-hand experience himself strengthens our position. We have felt that.

Nepal’s diplomats keep talking about cross-border early-warning cooperation with China and India. The Prime Minister raised it at the UN General Assembly. Is there progress?

We had a bilateral meeting with the Chinese delegation. We discussed how to take forward what the Prime Minister proposed on a Nepal–India–China initiative, and said it could start with research institutions in China and Nepal. China has supported Nepal on the mountain agenda, and that support has been immense. It came up in our bilateral meeting. We are working on how to move a trilateral forward, and we raised this on the sidelines. We are also meeting the Indian minister, and we will build on the support we have.

Eventually Nepal has to justify COP31 to the public. What would you count as a success?

Three things in the cover decision’s text. The language on the dedicated mountain work programme should explicitly define its scope and modalities. The two agreed mountain dialogues should sit under that programme. And the high-level political dialogue on mountains and climate change should be established, so the political discourse has a place to continue. The agenda stays under discussion in the presidency’s consultations. If these elements are reflected, it would be a major win for Nepal, and it would become institutionalised.

COP28, 29, 30 and now 31: Nepal keeps pushing a stand-alone mountain agenda and hits the same wall. Does the playbook need a fundamental change?

Look at history. Andorra submitted a mountain agenda at COP28, and it ended up confined to an annual dialogue. This time, against the backdrop of Bhotekoshi, with global gravity behind it, we submitted on the eve of COP31, and it has gone much further. The agenda is alive and has not been dropped.

Of our four elements, the cover decision already has a dedicated mountain work programme on finance and capacity-building gaps. It is less than we asked for, which is why we keep stressing scope and modalities, a dialogue guided by the work programme’s framework, and a high-level political dialogue. The agenda is what we discuss, and we are pushing its three major elements through the cover decision.

title: Nepal, India to launch Ayodhya-Janakpur train service during PM Shah’s visit - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal, India to launch Ayodhya-Janakpur train service during PM Shah’s visit  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal and India are preparing to launch a direct train service between Ayodhya and Janakpur during Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s upcoming visit to India.

Shah is scheduled to travel to India on November 22, with the service expected to be inaugurated the following day, according to the Ministry of Infrastructure Development. Shah and his Indian counterpart, Narendra Modi, are expected to jointly inaugurate the service.

The two cities hold religious significance for Hindus, and plans to connect them by rail have been under discussion for years, said Sushil Babu Dhakal, head of the Development Assistance Coordination and Quality Division at the ministry. “Ayodhya is the birthplace of Lord Ram, and the idea of connecting it to Janakpur by rail has been discussed for a long time,” Dhakal said.

The rail journey between Janakpur and Ayodhya will cover 604 kilometres, of which only 28 kilometres lie in Nepal. The service will initially carry passengers using an 18-coach train.

It will operate once a week in the first phase. A senior ministry official said the train would arrive in Janakpur from Ayodhya one day before making its return journey.

Nepal does not have its own train, so India will operate the service. The frequency could be increased later depending on passenger demand, the official said.

India has already built the railway infrastructure in Nepal with grant assistance. “For now, the service will be operated and managed by the Indian government,” the official said. “The operator will bear the costs of using the infrastructure on the Nepali side from Jayanagar.”

Electric trains currently run as far as Jayanagar in India, but the section inside Nepal is served by diesel-powered trains. During Shah’s visit, Nepal is preparing to ask India to provide grant assistance to electrify the railway infrastructure on the Nepali side, a ministry source said.

“Electric trains run up to Jayanagar, but the infrastructure on the Nepali side has not been electrified,” the source said.

Rohit Kumar Bisural, a former director general of the Department of Railways, welcomed the plan, saying the service would strengthen the cultural ties between the two countries.

“Ayodhya-Janakpur is a religious route. Our cultural ties go back a long way, and a train service will strengthen them further,” he said. Many Nepalis travel to Ayodhya, while pilgrims from India visit Janakpur. A direct service would make the journey quicker and more convenient, he added.

People currently travel between the two cities by various means. The railway link is expected to make the journey easier, although the service will initially operate on a limited schedule.

Bisural said the two governments should work towards making it a regular service and extending Nepal’s railway connections to other Indian cities.

“Railway connectivity with other Indian cities should also be expanded. The railway network is being extended towards Bardibas, with plans to eventually connect it to Kathmandu. Both governments should work together to advance that goal,” he said.

Nepal currently operates passenger trains along the 52-kilometre Jayanagar-Janakpur-Bijalpura section. The full Jayanagar-Bardibas railway line is planned to cover 69 kilometres, leaving 17 kilometres yet to be completed.

title: Nepal’s stolen Uma-Maheshvara statues belong back in their shrines - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal’s stolen Uma-Maheshvara statues belong back in their shrines  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
On 7 February 2022, a 12th-century Uma-Maheshvara stele was reinstalled at Tangal Hiti, a stone water spout in Patan. It was stolen from there in the 1980s. The New York-based Metropolitan Museum of Art had received it as a donation in 1983 and returned it to Nepal in 2018. It took almost four years to reinstall it in Patan. Its eventual return to the shrine is a model for what restitution should mean.

It is rarely what happens. Of the artefacts returned from the United States in recent years, one is back in its shrine and two remain in museum galleries, while another sits in the British Museum without so much as a verified reply. The object has to return to the community that worshipped it every morning.

A statue of an 18th century Uma-Maheshvara in Sundhara, Patan. Photo: Courtesy of Stolen Images of Nepal

Hindus worship Uma-Maheshvara as Shiva and Parvati seated together, an image of cosmic balance in which feminine and masculine energies complete each other. NR Banerjee, the Indian archaeologist and art historian who studied Nepal’s art, and architecture, called it arguably the country’s most beloved iconographic theme. Artists poured their best work into it from the Lichhavi period (c 400-879 CE) through the Malla period (1200-1769 CE).

Uma-Maheshvara iconography

Lain Singh Bangdel, the Nepali artist and art historian, identifies the oldest surviving example as a broken relief at Patan’s Chamunda Temple, dated to the third century. It shows a simple, two-handed Shiva and Parvati seated in lalitasana, the relaxed pose with one leg pendant. Over the centuries, the iconography grew more elaborate.

The most crowded compositions came between the 10th and 15th centuries: Uma (Parvati) seated at his left, Maheshvara (Shiva) with four hands—a rosary in one, a flower in another, his front right hand in varadamudra (granting boons) or sometimes abhayamudra (gesture of fearlessness) and another embracing her or sometimes resting on his knee. A parasol often crowns the scene, Ganga descends to the right, a celestial figure flies in with a garland, and Nandi, the bull, at his feet. Along the base, ganas , Shiva’s attendants, dance around Ganesha. Bangdel notes the waistband ( udarabandha ) as a distinctly Nepali marker. By the 18th century, the form had returned to quiet: a solitary pair with their mounts, the bull and the lion.

A valley tradition centuries old

Open-air stone sculptures like these have been vanishing from Nepal’s valleys since the 1960s. Until the night each disappeared, it stood in temple courtyards or above a hiti , where neighbours collected water, offered flowers and abhir , and prayed for harmony and prosperity.

The Uma-Maheshvara of Ganesh Temple, Pulchowk, 12th century, stolen in 1985. Photo: Courtesy of Stolen Images of Nepal

Kanak Mani Dixit, the writer and founding editor of Himal Southasian, wrote in ‘Gods in Exile’ (1999) that the craftsmanship that makes these images devotionally powerful also made them desirable to collectors. An 11th-century Uma-Maheshvara image above a hiti at Nasamana, Bhaktapur, vanished on 23 May, 1984 and now sits in Paris’s Musée Guimet. No replica was installed, and the spout has stood empty since.

Once stolen, the daily ritual does not travel with the object. A living presence becomes an exhibit behind glass, cut off from the community that gave it meaning.

The record of loss and the returns

The Uma-Maheshvara of Thapahiti, Patan, which is currently at the British Museum. Photo: Courtesy of Stolen Images of Nepal

Bangdel’s 1989 book ‘Stolen Images of Nepal’ documented 15 missing Uma-Maheshvara statues. Three have since been recovered locally, three returned from abroad, and nine remain unidentified. Some cases:

Wotu, Dhulikhel : Stolen in 1982 and purchased by Berlin’s Museum für Indische Kunst in 1985, it was returned to Nepal on 28 August 2000. Judged as too insecure for the shrine, it sits in the Patan Museum while a replica receives daily worship.

Gahiti, Patan : Stolen in the mid-1960s, it reached the Denver Art Museum on loan in the 1970s and as a gift in 1980. The museum returned it in September, 2021. It currently sits at the National Museum, Chhauni.

Chyasa Falcha, Patan : The group Lost Arts of Nepal identified this 1588 statue from a 1970 photograph. The Brooklyn Museum, which had held it since 1991, returned it on 31 January, 2024. It has been reinstalled at its shrine.

Thapahiti, Patan : Stolen in the late 1960s and replaced by a replica, the original is in the British Museum, which lists a 1970 purchase from Spink and Son Ltd. Matched in May 2023, it prompted the Department of Archaeology to write to the relevant parties in September. The museum has given no verified response.

The oldest surviving Uma-Maheshvara at Chamunda Temple, Patan, 3rd century. Photo: Courtesy of Stolen Images of Nepal

The law is on Nepal’s side. The Ancient Monument Preservation Act, 1956, bars exporting, relocating or collecting any historical or artistic object without government approval. A museum that bought from a dealer, a dealer who bought it from a smuggler, who took it from an active shrine, holds stolen property, however many hands it passed through. A thief cannot sell what he never owned, and institutions claiming good faith should explain why so many resist publishing full provenance. A clean transaction has nothing to hide.

Nor is restitution a gift. Returning a stolen deity is not charity extended to Nepal. It’s a correction of something that should never have happened in the first place.

Following the trail

The search is growing. An inventory of what is missing helps investigators, journalists and groups like Lost Arts of Nepal match images against catalogues and collections before the Department of Archaeology, which has legal standing, makes the formal claim. Ordinary travellers help as well. Someone who photographs an unmistakably Nepali object abroad and sends it to a scholar has already set off real cases.

Uma-Maheshvara from Wotu, Dhulikhel, currently housed at Patan Museum. Photo: Courtesy of Stolen Images of Nepal

Replicas, like the 50 in the Rabindra Puri Foundation’s Museum of Stolen Arts, keep the losses visible. A replica can keep the worship alive, as at Wotu, but it is a stopgap, not a remedy. Museums with gaps in their ownership history should not wait for Nepal to prove its claim. They should open their files and let the evidence lead them home.

Transit to the real place

Our heritage is living, and a successful return should not end with the statue sitting in a museum, just a Nepali one instead of a foreign one. These objects have been away for decades, and the absence has not stopped hurting because the state has grown used to it. For a deity worshipped every morning, a glass case in Kathmandu offers no more connection than one abroad. The distance that matters is devotional, not geographic.

title: Nepali Congress Faces Internal Division Amidst Leadership Struggles - Ratopati
description: Nepali Congress Faces Internal Division Amidst Leadership Struggles  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Nepali Congress is a party that has been active in Nepal's politics, democracy, and in the direction of changing the country for a long time. This party was established by Bisheshwor Prasad Koirala and is moving forward carrying the ideology he espoused. The Congress has gone through splits and divisions in the past and has reached this point. Now, once again, the Congress is on the verge of disintegration.

After the Genji rebellion, Gagan Thapa and others suddenly felt that they had to take leadership into their hands, otherwise the party would not survive. Under their leadership, a special general convention was held. After that general convention, they held the 15th general convention. From the general convention, some positions were unopposed and in most, a new working committee has been formed through elections.

From the general convention, they have made the office bearers a 25-member body. Although they said they would bring about extensive changes in the party with youth leadership, now not only the youth but also the old guard have been included. Overall, three generations are visible in the Congress. From the general convention, a young dynamic leadership like Gaganji, a leadership with ideology, not only kept two posts of party president but also compromised on all other posts and issues and moved forward. This is not good for the party.

Although there is one party president, the remaining posts have increased from two, four to fifteen. It is evident from this general convention that positions have been created based on the faces and appearances of those who need to be brought into the central committee and office bearers.

If ideology cannot bind the cadres, then positions cannot hold anyone in the party. People wander in search of opportunities. There is no guarantee that expanding the organization into a jumbo size will increase votes, make the party popular, or bring back lost public support. Ideology is a big thing in politics. Morality, values, principles, ideals are big things. If positions are created through bargaining like this, going beyond those moral values and principles, the condition of the Congress is likely to become the same as that of the Communists. Even though the Communist parties have formed central committees of more than 600 people, did they get an equal number of seats in the elections? No.

Our society is currently enjoying populism. It is running after the popularity of the leadership. Society deifies someone as a god in the first 2 years.

The seats won by winning the hearts of the people and getting votes are not obtained by making the working committee, the central working committee jumbo and creating many positions. The party does not become big by having a large working committee and many office bearers. A party runs on ideology. Currently, the cadres from the center to the ward level are confused about where the politics of the Congress is heading. Politics is philosophy, sacrifice, dedication. Not only that, politics is about good and liberal tendencies and systems, which the Congress has not been able to explain to its cadres.

It has been said that the influence of 'Don-ism' and 'money-ism' has always been significant in Congress. That influence still remains as it is. Currently, those who have received tickets in Congress and have been elected to the central working committee, apart from the representation of the communities for whom their respective clusters are designated, are dominated by the influential. On the other hand, who do we call youth again? Those who have been MPs five or six times, but hold the belief that only the Prime Minister and party president should be for two terms, are they youth? These are not arguments, in my opinion, they are just fallacies.

There is no such thing as 'this many years' in politics. Politics is about sacrifice and dedication. It can be seen in the world that those who engage in politics until they live can provide service. Did Malaysia, America, and Singapore develop under the leadership of young people aged 20, 30, and 40? Certainly not. All were developed by the 'vision' of leaders aged 60, 70, and 80. One should be allowed to do politics as long as their body is healthy, their mind is healthy, and their thoughts are healthy. In politics, the idea of 'you have eaten for this many years, now it's my turn' indicates something is wrong.

Our society is currently enjoying populism. It is running after the popularity of the leadership. Society deifies someone as a god in the first 2 years. That same society does not hesitate to demonize the same person after two years. This is a challenge. Currently, the Nepali Congress appears to be divided into two. Leaders like Dr. Shekhar Koirala, Sher Bahadur Deuba, Dr. Shashank Koirala, who came from the regular general convention team, are saying that we are legitimate. They are saying that Gagan Thapa and others have snatched the party's legitimacy. The Election Commission and the joint bench of the Supreme Court gave legitimacy to Gaganji. Against that, the Supreme Court has given a stay order to Sher Bahadur and others. This is causing accusations and counter-accusations within the Congress.

People who followed Purna Bahadur have now become Gagan's favorites. It is laughable in itself that those who proposed to immediately take action against Gagan and Bishwa are now dear to Gagan.

Elections are coming. Congress will have to struggle hard to win, which is difficult, but not impossible to lose. Gaganji and others are talking about Congress 2.0. The party does not become strong by writing slogans and singing songs. For strength, leadership must be liberal. Citizens are watching how the leadership behaves when in power and out of power. Gaganji would have become the party president even if he had held a regular general convention. Anyone could have competed with him, but there was not much competition, but despite being popular, he hurried too much. As a result, the Congress could not remain united. Unfortunately, because the Congress did not remain united, he is now facing accusations on social media. He is being targeted by his own party colleagues. This is his weakness. It is the weakness of the leadership. Leadership should always embrace everyone.

On the other hand, why couldn't Bishwa-ji and Gagan-ji hold the general convention when they were about to become general secretaries? Why couldn't they make decisions on time? Many people are accusing them of withholding the details of active membership. When one is about to hold an important position, the party president says that everything was ruined, we were not allowed to do anything. This was wrong. Sher Bahadur Deuba has made mistakes, and he has. Purna Bahadur Khadka had many mistakes. Purna Bahadur is responsible for bringing about this situation. Instead of communicating with Gaganji repeatedly to hold the general convention, Purna Bahadur deceived Sher Bahadur as well and kept him engaged in delaying tactics. Now, the same Purna Bahadur is trying to become Gaganji's favorite. It is laughable in itself that those who proposed to immediately take action against Gagan and Bishwa are now dear to Gagan.

Everyone's hope and trust lie with Congress. Congress embraces everyone, provides social justice, and the Congress that established democracy must also preserve it, but the leadership is starting to forget this. The leadership needs to be reminded of this. Gaganji and others might remember, but it will be too late. Because his half group, brothers, will have already started forming a separate party by holding a separate general convention. Whether the legitimacy will be with whom, the court's decision will tell. Even if Gaganji gets the legitimacy, it will be difficult for the party to remain united. This was something the leadership needed to understand upon reaching the top, but they did not understand.

On the other hand, Gaganji's attempt to increase seats was based on the assumption that all people from Sher Bahadur's team would come. The main reason for creating a jumbo central working committee seems to be the thought that if I open up many seats, everyone from Deuba's side will come, and there will be enough seats for everyone. He thought about which clusters to add people from to shift Deuba's faction, without considering whether this would benefit or harm the party. He did not pay attention to where the jumbo central working committee meeting would be held. The respect that used to be associated with being a central member of Congress has been lost.

How can we say that a person who has come after organizing such a large group, who has been an MP and minister so many times, and who aspires to be the Prime Minister, does not understand these things? But he made a mistake. The situation may come to regret.

title: Nepal-India border dispute back in focus ahead of Balen’s India visit - OnlineKhabar English News
description: Nepal-India border dispute back in focus ahead of Balen’s India visit  OnlineKhabar English News

full_article:
PM Balen Shah

Kathmandu, November 16

As Prime Minister Balendra Shah prepares for his upcoming visit to India, former diplomats and border experts have urged him to make Nepal’s long-standing border disputes a priority in talks with the Indian leadership.

They say the visit offers an opportunity to revive diplomatic dialogue that has remained stalled for years, particularly over Kalapani, Lipulekh, Limpiyadhura and Susta.

The dispute intensified in November 2019, when India’s Survey of India published the seventh edition of its political map following the separation of Ladakh from Jammu and Kashmir. Nepal objected after the map included Kalapani, Lipulekh and Limpiyadhura within Indian territory.

Nepal sent three diplomatic notes through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, but India did not respond.

Tensions escalated further in May 2020, when Indian Defence Minister Rajnath Singh inaugurated a road connecting Pithoragarh in Uttarakhand to Lipulekh via Nepal’s Gunji area. The road was intended to facilitate the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage in Tibet.

Nepal protested the move and called for dialogue to resolve the border dispute. However, India did not respond positively to its efforts. In May 2020, Nepal’s Parliament endorsed a revised political map incorporating Limpiyadhura, Lipulekh and Kalapani. The move further strained relations between the two countries.

A diplomatic mechanism that never became functional

The current border dispute could perhaps have been contained had an agreement reached during Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s first visit to Nepal in August 2014 been implemented.

During the visit, then Prime Minister Sushil Koirala and Modi agreed to establish a mechanism led by the foreign secretaries of both countries to address outstanding border issues, particularly in Kalapani and Susta.

A joint statement issued on August 4, 2014, said the two prime ministers had welcomed the decision of the Joint Commission to direct the foreign secretaries to work on unresolved border issues, including Kalapani and Susta, with technical support from the Boundary Working Group (BWG) as necessary.

However, the foreign secretary-level mechanism never held a meeting.

Former Nepali ambassador to India Nilamber Acharya believes the border dispute would not have reached its current level had the mechanism been made functional.

“If there had been continuous dialogue, the border dispute between the two neighbours might not have reached this level,” Acharya said. “Had the secretary-level mechanism functioned, disagreements from both sides could have been discussed in those meetings, potentially paving the way for a solution.”

Acharya, who was also a member of the Eminent Persons’ Group (EPG) formed to review Nepal-India relations and recommend ways to improve them, says Shah should clearly communicate Nepal’s position on the border issue during his visit.

“Some problems may not be resolved overnight, but the border issue should not be left pending. The prime minister must clearly say that dialogue needs to begin,” he said.

Two different kinds of border disputes

A road being constructed by India in Susta, Nepal-India border area, in January 2022.

Experts say Nepal must first clearly identify the nature of its border disputes before deciding which issues to prioritise during the visit.

Nepal and India share a border of approximately 1,880 kilometres, with disputes broadly falling into two categories.

The first concerns territorial claims and alleged encroachment. The main disputed areas are Kalapani and Susta. Both Nepal and India have formally acknowledged that disputes exist in these locations.

Under the 1816 Treaty of Sugauli, the territory east of the Kali (Mahakali) River belongs to Nepal. Nepal maintains that the river originates at Limpiyadhura and therefore claims the Limpiyadhura-Kalapani-Lipulekh area as its territory.

India, however, does not accept the river originating at Limpiyadhura as the Mahakali. Its official maps identify different streams as the Kali River. Indian security forces are also stationed in Kalapani.

The second category involves cross-border encroachment and disputes over the no-man’s land, or the area between the two countries’ border lines. These include damaged or missing boundary pillars and encroachment into the no-man’s land.

Experts say such disputes can largely be addressed through meetings of the Nepal-India Joint Working Group on Border Management, led by officials at the joint secretary level.

Former ambassador Acharya cautions against mixing the two categories.

“Territorial encroachment and disputes over the no-man’s land are different issues. The first thing is to be clear about what each dispute involves,” he said.

Balen’s parliamentary remarks sparked controversy

Prime Minister Shah’s remarks in the House of Representatives on May 31 also brought the border issue into political controversy.

Responding to a question from CPN-UML lawmaker Padma Aryal about the construction of a trade route by India and China through a bilateral understanding, Shah said he had recently learned after becoming prime minister that Nepal had not only faced encroachment by India but had also encroached on considerable Indian territory.

His remarks prompted opposition parties to obstruct parliamentary proceedings.

Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal later clarified that Shah was referring to cross-border encroachment. Parliament resumed after the clarification, although the opposition’s demand to remove the prime minister’s remarks from the parliamentary record was not met.

Shah subsequently attempted to clarify his position at the Rastriya Swatantra Party’s Chitwan convention, saying Nepal had evidence to support its claims over Kalapani and Lipulekh, without referring directly to his earlier parliamentary remarks.

In 2023, when he was mayor of Kathmandu Metropolitan City, Shah had also displayed a map of Greater Nepal in his office amid controversy over the ‘Akhand Bharat’ map displayed in India’s new Parliament building.

Experts call for evidence-based preparation

Former ambassador Dinesh Bhattarai says the government does not appear to have undertaken adequate preparations for Shah’s proposed visit in the first week of Mangsir.

“Given the number of issues that need to be discussed with India, I have not seen evidence of comprehensive consultations ahead of the visit,” Bhattarai said.

He added that the prime minister must first have a clear understanding of the border dispute and prepare to present Nepal’s position at the highest political level with supporting evidence.

One unresolved issue is the signing of 182 strip maps jointly prepared by Nepal and India. The maps cover almost the entire border, but their formal endorsement has remained pending because of the disputes over Kalapani and Susta.

Border experts say formalising the strip maps could resolve around 98 per cent of the boundary-related issues between the two countries.

Bangladesh offers a lesson in resolving border disputes

Experts say resolving the Nepal-India border dispute is not impossible, pointing to the example of India and Bangladesh.

The two countries implemented their Land Boundary Agreement in 2015, resolving decades of disputes over enclaves and territorial boundaries. Under the agreement, India received 7,110 acres of land, while Bangladesh received 17,160 acres.

The settlement followed decades of diplomatic efforts. India had not ratified the 1974 land boundary agreement signed by Indian Prime Minister Indira Gandhi and Bangladeshi leader Sheikh Mujibur Rahman.

Bangladesh continued pursuing the issue, and a settlement was eventually reached more than four decades later, during the premiership of Mujibur Rahman’s daughter, Sheikh Hasina.

Experts say Nepal should draw lessons from Bangladesh’s sustained diplomatic efforts rather than allowing its border disputes to remain unresolved because of India’s reluctance.

Nepal and China settled their border dispute through dialogue

Nepal’s experience with China also demonstrates how sustained high-level engagement can resolve sensitive territorial disagreements.

The two countries established diplomatic relations in 1955 and settled their border dispute within a few years. Prime Minister BP Koirala held five rounds of discussions with Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai before Nepal and China signed their boundary treaty on October 5, 1961.

The agreement followed the resolution of a dispute over the ownership of Mount Everest.

Bhattarai says Koirala’s preparation was instrumental in reaching the agreement.

“BP Koirala used to explain the issues at the negotiating table with the help of maps. Prime Minister Balen, who has received such a strong mandate, should also prepare himself to present Nepal’s position with similar clarity,” he said.

However, the tri-junction where the borders of Nepal, India and China meet remains undetermined. Nepal and China could not establish the point in the absence of India, and the unresolved issue has repeatedly resurfaced in disputes over Lipulekh.

Tri-junction must be a priority

The issue gained renewed attention in April this year after India and China agreed to reopen the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage route through Lipulekh, which Nepal claims as its territory.

India maintains that it has been using the route for the pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet since 1954. However, when India and China signed the Sino-Indian Agreement that year, Nepal had not yet established diplomatic relations with China.

The two neighbours had also decided to use Lipulekh without consulting Nepal following the 2015 earthquake. The Sushil Koirala-led government at the time sent diplomatic notes to both countries protesting the decision.

Border expert Buddhi Narayan Shrestha says Shah should give priority to establishing the tri-junction during his visit to New Delhi.

“The issue of establishing the tri-junction, which could not be determined in India’s absence at the time, must be given top priority by Prime Minister Balendra,” Shrestha said.

Mahesh Bhatt, a member of the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party’s Department of International Relations and Diplomacy, says preparations for the visit are progressing.

“The foreign minister, who also heads the party’s international department, has just returned after participating in COP. Although the preparations have not taken a concrete public shape, internal work is progressing rapidly,” Bhatt said.

Experts say that clear priorities, adequate preparation and sustained diplomatic engagement will be essential if Shah’s visit is to make progress on Nepal’s long-standing border concerns.
